canonical.definition: The internal experience of running a company — motivation, resilience, burnout, self-doubt, and the personal operating habits founders build to sustain themselves through setbacks.
Holding and acting on a belief the market or peers reject, including how founders reason from first principles to earn that belief and when stubbornness becomes delusion.
Choosing what to build and when, based on which technology shift has just made a previously impossible or unattractive problem viable.
Shortening the build–measure–learn cycle — in software, hardware, design, or research — treated as the startup's primary competitive lever rather than an efficiency nicety.
How early-stage companies find, assess, and evaluate people — funnel design, work-sample assessment, who holds the hiring decision, and post-hire performance evaluation.
Deliberately keeping headcount low and raising output per person — via AI tooling, talent density, and decision structures that survive without consensus — as a company-design choice.
Deciding how much to raise, against which milestones, and how to spend it — runway planning, value inflection points, and the cost accounting of expensive experiments.
Building startups whose core risk is scientific or physical rather than market — long R&D timelines, capital intensity, manufacturing, and the strategy choices those force.
A startup treating regulation as a solvable part of the product — permitting, approvals, and compliance sequencing — including when incumbent-favoring rules are the real barrier to entry.
How AI rules actually get made and what they say — legislative and agency process, federal versus state authority, compute thresholds, IP law, and public R&D funding.
Arguments about severe downside from increasingly capable models — loss of control, dual-use capability, recursive self-improvement, concentration of power, and labor displacement.
Releasing weights, code, or tooling openly as a deliberate competitive and ecosystem play, including the maintainership burden and governance that follow.
Building on a platform — especially a foundation model lab — that can absorb your product, change your economics, or cut your access, and how startups position against that.
aliases: platform risk from foundation model labs

canonical.definition: Founders using public visibility — building in public, personal brand, and earned attention — as a distribution channel and hiring magnet rather than a vanity exercise.
The hands-on practice of designing what users see and touch — icons, type, marks, metaphor, and constraint — and the process of generating, critiquing, and presenting options.
The lean-startup loop of talking to users, shipping a minimum viable product, and letting observed demand rather than a plan drive the next build.
AI systems that perceive and act in the physical world — robots, vehicles, and machines — including generalist robot foundation models, end-to-end policies, and transfer across embodiments.
Using simulated environments to design, train, or validate physical systems, and closing the gap between simulated behavior and real-world performance.
Engineering systems whose failures hurt people — redundancy, sensor diversity, nines of uptime, and the long distance between an impressive demo and a deployable product.
Extracting latent capability from models already trained — un-hobbling, scaffolding, and post-training — on the premise that deployed systems lag what the weights can already do.
The argument that general methods which scale with compute beat hand-engineered structure, and the counter-pressure from data-efficient and distilled approaches.
The judgment that decides which experiments and problems are worth pursuing, and the operating model a lab or founder builds around that judgment.
The physical substrate of AI — specialized inference hardware, accelerated computing, and the energy and data-movement costs that set the ceiling on what can be served.
Treating what you measure and how as proprietary advantage — owning domain-specific evals and surrogate scorers — and the way public benchmarks saturate and stop discriminating.
Agents built for one individual's life and work — accumulating that person's context, acting proactively on their behalf — rather than a shared product for many users.
The engineering of the scaffold around a model — loop, prompts, tools, memory, and control flow — treated as the primary unit of design and iteration, distinct from the model itself.
The practice of deciding what information enters a model's context and in what form, treating context assembly as a first-class engineering discipline rather than prompt wording.
Persisting and recalling information across an agent's turns, sessions, or lifetime — storage substrate, write policy, and retrieval policy.
How engineers actually work with coding agents day to day — delegation patterns, review rhythm, parallelism, and the shape of the resulting dev loop.
Work that spans many steps, hours, or days, where the difficulty comes from horizon length — accumulated error, state, and coherence — not per-step difficulty.
Checked-in files that persistently steer an agent's behavior — rules, instructions, and voice — as versioned artifacts a team edits together.
Spending more compute at inference — longer reasoning, sampling, or search — to buy accuracy without changing weights.
Managing the unit economics of serving models — cost per token, per query, and per agent run — as a first-order product constraint.
Agents running the scientific loop — hypothesis generation, experiment design, analysis — in research and biomedical domains.
Untrusted content in an agent's context hijacking its instructions, and the mitigations for it; covers both the attack and the defenses.
Selling and distributing AI products — positioning, ICP, sales motion, pricing models, and developer-led distribution.

drop_guidance: Drop bare field labels that name a speaker's industry rather than a transferable idea, unless the talk generalizes from them — 'quantum information science' and 'brain-computer interfaces' should only land on deep tech company building when used as an exemplar of deep-tech company building; otherwise drop.

Drop biographical or single-datapoint anecdotes: 'dropping out of college', 'new business formation data'. These are evidence inside one talk, not concepts other talks can engage, and would produce dead one-talk pages.

Never keep lexical or case variants as separate pages — 'physical ai' / 'physical AI', 'agent harness' / 'harness design' / 'agent harness engineering', 'long-horizon agents' / 'long-horizon agent runs'. Collapse to the canonical name.

Map over-specific one-off techniques up to their parent rather than minting: 'metadata conditioning' and 'human intervention in data collection' → physical ai; 'system prompt ablation' → capability elicitation; 'bitmap typography' → product and visual design craft. Drop only if the parent already fully covers the string and it adds no distinct sense.

Drop strings that merely restate the event's framing or a talk's subject rather than an idea — e.g. 'frontier lab operating model' when it is only describing one lab's org chart (otherwise map to research taste).

Drop generic business-function strings with no AI or startup-stage specificity if no parent claims them; 'performance review design' belongs on founder hiring bar only because it is framed as an early-stage evaluation problem.
notes:
Deliberate separations: (1) 'founder psychology' (resilience, burnout, sustaining yourself) is kept apart from 'contrarian conviction' (non-consensus belief and judgment) — a burnout story is not a conviction story. (2) 'regulatory navigation for startups' (a company routing around or through rules) is kept apart from 'ai policy and regulation' (how the rules themselves get made); a talk by a policymaker goes to the latter, a founder describing FDA/permitting goes to the former. (3) 'ai compute infrastructure' (hardware, energy, physical ceiling) is kept apart from the reused 'inference cost optimization' (per-token unit economics as a product constraint). (4) 'simulation and sim-to-real transfer' was minted rather than reusing AIEWF's 'simulation environments', which is scoped to exercising software agents and simulated users, not physical-system design and embodiment gap. (5) 'iteration speed' spans software, hardware, and design deliberately — it is the cross-domain claim, not a hardware-only concept.

Deliberate merges: 'robot foundation models', 'cross-embodiment transfer', 'end-to-end models', and robot training-data strings all fold into 'physical ai' because this event has too few robotics/AV talks to support separate pages; if assignment finds three or more talks distinctly discussing generalist robot policies, splitting 'robot foundation models' back out is the right call. 'spec-driven development' and 'agentic loop design' exist as exact AIEWF concepts but appear in only one talk each here, so they were folded into 'agentic coding workflows' and 'agent harness design' respectively — cross-event links to those AIEWF pages can still be made from the parent.

Ambiguous boundaries the assignment pass will hit: 'eval and metrics as moat' was placed on 'platform dependency risk' (defensibility against labs) rather than 'evaluation as competitive moat' — if the talk's argument is about measurement practice rather than defensibility, move it. 'agent controllability' sits on 'frontier ai risk' (steerability as a safety property), not on harness design. 'code review as risk management' sits on 'agentic coding workflows' but shades into 'prompt injection defense' when the untrusted input is the agent's own output. 'prompt injection defense' is a thin reuse here (2 aliases, ~2-3 talks) — kept because the cross-event link is worth more than the page density; drop it if assignment finds fewer than three talks.
